title: The Dam Didn't Fail. The Mountain Did.
subs: In the summer of 1959, a young geologist
named Edoardo Semenza was mapping the slopes
of a mountain in the Italian Alps.
Below him, one of the tallest dams in the world was almost finished.
The engineer who had designed that dam was his father.
What Edoardo found in the rock suggested that
an entire mountainside was not as solid as it appeared.
It bore the scars of an enormous prehistoric landslide,
one that had already fallen thousands of years
earlier and could move again.
Four years later, on the night of October 9, 1963,
it did.
Around 260 million cubic metres of rock
slid into the lake behind the dam in less than a minute.
An enormous wave surged across the reservoir,
poured over the top of the dam, and destroyed the town below.
Almost 2,000 people were killed.
The dam itself survived with remarkably little damage.
It is still standing today.
This is the story of Vajont, and of how a structure
could be engineered with extraordinary precision
and still stand at the centre of the deadliest
landslide disaster in Europe's recorded history.
